## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="m8-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Here and now, then recourse</dt><dd>The size is chosen before the build-out is known; the operation in each branch is chosen after.</dd>
<dt>Wait and see</dt><dd>Each branch's own best plan: 380, 1,300 or 2,220 MW. No single plan is best in every branch.</dd>
<dt>Plan for the average</dt><dd>1,300 MW, sized for 5,000 MW of wind; it expects $662.63M a year but costs $673.72M over the branches.</dd>
<dt>Stochastic program</dt><dd>845 MW, the lowest expected cost: $671.10M a year.</dd>
<dt>Two values</dt><dd>Value of the stochastic solution $2.62M a year; expected value of perfect information $17.56M a year.</dd>
<dt>Robust plans</dt><dd>Worst case 380 MW (worst cost $703.40M); least regret 942.3 MW (largest regret $35.87M). Neither uses the chances.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The extensive form in algebra, and the order of the costs</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

For branches $s \in \{\text{none}, \text{half}, \text{all}\}$ and wind blocks $b = 1 \dots 5$, one linear program holds the size and every branch's operation (the extensive form, also called the deterministic equivalent):

$$\min_{x,\,e,\,r}\; c\,x + \sum_s p_s \sum_b h_b\, c_r\, r_{s,b}$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
k\,e_{s,b} + r_{s,b} &= H && \text{(hydrogen, every branch and block)}\\
e_{s,b} &\le x && \text{(the size links the stages)}\\
0 \le e_{s,b} &\le \sigma_{s,b} = \max(0,\; W_s f_b - A), \quad r_{s,b} \ge 0,\; x \ge 0
\end{aligned}
$$

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| $x$ | electrolyzer size, chosen here and now | MW |
| $c$ | yearly cost of a MW of electrolyzer | \$80,000 |
| $p_s$ | chance of branch $s$ | 0.25, 0.5, 0.25 |
| $h_b$, $f_b$ | hours a year and wind capacity factor of block $b$ | 500 to 3,760 h; 0.571 to 0.194 |
| $e_{s,b}$, $r_{s,b}$ | electrolyzer power (MW) and reformer hydrogen (kg an hour): recourse | |
| $k$, $H$, $c_r$ | 18 kg per MWh; 54,000 kg an hour; \$1.50 per kg | |
| $W_s$, $A$ | wind built in branch $s$; what the lines take | 3,000, 5,000, 7,000 MW; 1,000 MW |

- **Size.** 31 columns and 30 rows; with $n$ branches it has $1 + 10n$ columns, so it grows with every branch you add.
- **The order of the costs.** WS ≤ RP ≤ EEV: here \$653.54M ≤ \$671.10M ≤ \$673.72M. So EVPI = RP − WS and VSS = EEV − RP are both zero or more ([Birge and Louveaux, ch. 4](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4614-0237-4)).
- **Robust plans.** Add a free variable $z$ and minimise it, with $z \ge \text{cost}_s(x)$ in every branch (worst case), or $z \ge \text{cost}_s(x) - \text{WS}_s$ (least regret). Neither row uses $p_s$.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Why 845 MW: the critical-hours rule</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **One more MW.** It costs \$80,000 a year and saves \$1.50 × 18 = \$27 for every hour it runs on surplus. It pays while it runs more than \$80,000 ÷ \$27 = 2,963 hours a year.
- **In each branch.** Below 380 MW (none built), 1,300 MW (half) or 2,220 MW (all), an extra MW runs 3,000 hours; just above, 1,500. Each wait-and-see plan sits where its count falls below 2,963.
- **Over the branches.** Weighted by the chances, an extra MW just below 845 MW runs 3,750 hours; just above, 2,750. The stochastic plan sits where the expected count crosses 2,963.
- **When the rule stops.** With one size, no storage and one zone, this rule finds the plan by hand. A tank, several zones or pipelines couple the blocks and the sizes; then only the linear program finds it.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this toy leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Risk: the stochastic plan weighs only expected cost. A planner who fears the bad branches can add a risk measure, such as the expected cost of the worst 10% of outcomes.</li>
<li>Later decisions: here the size is chosen once. A multi-stage program lets the planner build more after part of the uncertainty resolves.</li>
<li>Where the branches come from: three hand-picked branches with judged chances. More branches drawn by sampling bring sampling error, as in <a href="m07-monte-carlo.html">M7</a>.</li>
<li>Time: five blocks of a duration curve, so no storage and no hour-to-hour links. Representative periods with storage are <a href="m03-capacity-expansion.html">M3</a>'s subject.</li>
<li>Space: one zone, no pipelines, steady hydrogen demand and a fixed price for reformer hydrogen.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself, then try it
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="m8-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="average" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Planning for the average future gives you the average cost.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Here the plan for 5,000 MW of wind expects $662.63M a year; priced in the three branches with their chances, it costs $673.72M.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="robust" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A robust plan is the best plan by every yardstick.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. The worst-case plan has the lowest worst cost, $703.40M, but it costs $12.16M a year more in expectation than the stochastic plan.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="evpi" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “The expected value of perfect information is what a real forecast of the build-out is worth.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It is the most a perfect forecast is worth, under these chances, to a planner who weighs only expected cost. A forecast that can be wrong is worth less.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="m8">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="values" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">The plan for the average costs $50M in expectation, the stochastic plan $48M, and the wait-and-see plans $45M weighted by their chances. VSS and EVPI?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">VSS $2M, EVPI $3M</li><li data-value="b">VSS $3M, EVPI $2M</li><li data-value="c">VSS $5M, EVPI $3M</li><li data-value="d">VSS $2M, EVPI $5M</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>VSS = $50M − $48M = $2M; EVPI = $48M − $45M = $3M.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="chances" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">You change the branches' chances. Which plan stays the same?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">The stochastic plan</li><li data-value="b">The plan for the average</li><li data-value="c">The worst-case plan</li><li data-value="d">All three move</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>The worst-case plan: it uses the set of build-outs, not their chances. Here it stays at 380 MW.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-case-try">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Try it yourself with open code</p>
<p class="lx-hint">Optional, about 30 minutes; needs Python 3.10 or later (<a href="b02-python-data.html">lesson B2</a>).</p>
<ul>
<li>Install the repository (its README's quick start), then run <code>python examples/minimal.py</code>: an invented four-zone region over three days, with a nine-branch tree.</li>
<li>Plan for one future: give <code>build_instance</code> the tree <code>ScenarioTree((Level("M", 1.0, 1.0),), (Level("M", 0.3, 1.0),))</code>. Which sizes change against the nine-branch plan?</li>
<li>Its objective is what that plan expects in its one future, as in step 4, not its cost across the nine branches.</li>
</ul>
<p><a href="https://github.com/Henryutd2021/txh2-ercot-hydrogen">txh2-ercot-hydrogen</a>: public example repository · MIT licence · synthetic data.</p>
</div>
```
